notes.meaning: Paul gives Timothy instructions on how to correct people gently. He must not strike an older man with sharp, angry words, but plead with him respectfully as a son would with his own father. Younger men should be corrected as brothers, with love and humility rather than a superior attitude.

Timothy must treat older women with the same tender respect he would show his mother. He must treat younger women like sisters, guarding his thoughts, speech, and actions with complete moral purity. This keeps a young minister safe from any hint of scandal or temptation.

The church must show special honor and care to widows who are truly in need. Honoring them means providing food, shelter, and financial help when they have no one else to turn to. The church family steps in to protect those who are completely alone in the world.

If a widow has children or grandchildren, caring for her is their responsibility rather than the church's. Taking care of an aged mother or grandmother is a natural way to repay her for years of loving care. God is deeply pleased when families practice their faith by supporting their own relatives.

A widow who is truly in need has no living relatives left to help her, so she places all her hope in God. Having no human support, she spends her days and nights crying out to the Lord in prayer. Her steady prayers serve the church even as she relies on God for daily provision.

A widow who lives only for luxury, pampering herself and chasing pleasure, is spiritually dead even though her body is still alive. Spending life merely indulging selfish desires misses the true purpose God gave her. Such a person should not receive the charitable support of the church.

Timothy must give these clear directions to the congregation so everyone knows their duty. When families provide for their own and the church supports only the truly needy, the community remains blameless. This prevents confusion, bad behavior, and false charges against the church.

Anyone who refuses to provide for their own family members has practically abandoned the Christian faith. True belief in God always shows itself in active love and family responsibility. Even unbelievers naturally care for their relatives, so a neglectful believer is acting worse than someone outside the church.

To be enrolled on the church's official list of widows, a woman had to be at least sixty years old and faithful to one husband. She also needed a proven track record of good deeds, such as raising children, welcoming travelers, humbly washing guests' feet, and helping the hurting. This enrollment was not just about receiving charity, but about joining a trusted group of older women recognized for lifelong Christian service.

Timothy is told not to put younger widows on this official roll of church workers. As time passes, their desires may change and lead them to want to marry again, drawing them away from their dedicated pledge of service to Christ. Breaking that original promise brings guilt and judgment upon them for abandoning their first commitment.

Without the daily responsibilities of a family, younger widows supported by the church risked falling into idleness. They were in danger of going from house to house, meddling in other people's affairs, and spreading gossip they had no right to share. Idleness often leads to harmful chatter that hurts church fellowship.

Paul advises younger widows to remarry, bear children, and manage their own households. Directing their energy into family life keeps them safely occupied and prevents them from falling into idle habits. Living an upright domestic life leaves no opening for enemies of the gospel to speak evil of the church.

Tragically, some younger widows had already turned away from following Christ and followed Satan into careless, sinful behavior. Paul gives these strict guidelines because real harm had already occurred in the community. Good boundaries help keep vulnerable believers from being trapped by the enemy.

Any Christian woman who has dependent widows in her family should support them herself. Taking care of family members lifts a heavy burden from the local church's funds. This allows the church to focus its resources on helping widows who are completely alone and have no other helper.

Elders who lead the church faithfully are worthy of high honor and generous financial support. This is especially true for those who pour their energy into preaching and teaching God's Word. Pastors who labor hard in ministry deserve both great respect and fair compensation.

differ.view: This verse describes two distinct church offices: ruling elders who govern the congregation, and teaching elders who preach and teach.
All elders hold a single office and must be able to teach, though some give more time and effort to preaching as their primary work.

notes.meaning: Scripture supports paying ministers for their work. Paul cites the Old Testament law that an ox must not be muzzled while treading out grain, showing that God expects working animals and people to eat. He also pairs this with Jesus' saying that a laborer deserves his wages, treating Christ's words as authoritative Scripture.

Timothy must not take an accusation against a church elder seriously unless it is backed by two or three witnesses. Because ministers must confront sin, they frequently face false rumors and bitter complaints. Requiring multiple witnesses protects innocent leaders from malicious attacks.

Leaders who continue in willful sin after being confronted must be rebuked in front of the entire assembly. Open sin in leadership causes widespread harm, so the correction must also be public. This firm discipline produces a healthy reverence and keeps others from falling into the same sin.

Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God, Jesus Christ, and the holy angels to carry out these discipline rules without bias. He must never prejudge a case before hearing all the evidence, nor favor friends or wealthy members. Church leaders must handle discipline with strict justice because heaven is watching.

Timothy must not rush to ordain anyone to church leadership by laying hands on them before their life and character are fully tested. Quickly appointing an ungodly leader makes the ordainer partly responsible for the sins that person commits in office. Timothy must keep his own life morally pure and separate from other people's sins.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Laying on hands here may refer to restoring disciplined, repentant sinners back into church fellowship rather than ordaining ministers.

notes.meaning: Timothy is urged to stop drinking only water and to take a little wine to help his weak stomach and frequent illnesses. True purity does not require harsh self-denial that damages bodily health. Taking reasonable care of one's physical body is important so that a minister can continue serving God effectively.

differ.view: Paul permits wine here solely as a medicinal remedy for sickness, not as an ordinary drink for Christians.
Scripture allows the moderate drinking of wine as a beverage, while condemning drunkenness.

notes.meaning: Some men's sins are completely obvious, pointing straight to judgment before any close investigation is needed. Other people's sins are well hidden and come to light only later or on the final judgment day. In the same way, good deeds are often easily seen, but even quiet and unnoticed good works will eventually be revealed by God.
